\title{A stabilizer-rank residual backend for \texttt{clifft}:\\
       an honest assessment on magic-sparse circuits}
\author{Research note (revised)}
\date{\today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\texttt{clifft} simulates Clifford$+T$ circuits with a symbolic Clifford frame
plus a dense $2^k$ active block. We build and validate a low-rank stabilizer
(CH-form) backend for the magic-sparse regime: minimal-extent $\{I,S\}$ magic
decomposition ($2^{0.228t}$), single-shot tensor-product magic sampling, BGH
norm estimation, and a global Clifford-frame composition, each checked against
a dense oracle and against \texttt{clifft} to machine precision. This revision
replaces the earlier draft's headline claim, which an adversarial review
refuted: the ``crossover at $n\!\approx\!22$'' was measured against
\texttt{clifft}'s \emph{unitary} path (peak rank $n$), while \texttt{clifft}'s
own \texttt{record\_probabilities} answers the same queries \emph{exactly} from
the measured program --- at peak rank $1$ on that benchmark's chain-IQP family
($\sim\!10^5\times$ faster than the number we charged it), and at peak rank
$n/2$ on dense random IQP. Re-benchmarked fairly (dense IQP, exact
$2^{n/2}$ baseline, exact meet-in-the-middle ground truth, and an error metric
that charges the \emph{full} pipeline), the true picture is: \texttt{clifft}'s
exact fast path wins to $n\!\approx\!34$; the backend overtakes at
$n\!\approx\!34$ for $\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.17$ and at $n\!\approx\!48$ for
$\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.08$, with a clean measured accuracy dial
$\mathrm{TV}=(0.50\pm0.01)\,\delta$; and beyond $n\!\approx\!62$ --- where every
exact method (dense block, forced replay, meet-in-the-middle) needs
$\gtrsim\!16$\,GB--$1$\,TB --- the backend is the only method that runs
($n{=}72$: $267$\,s, $1.9$\,GB, extrapolated $\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.18$). The
composition's ``free Clifford'' advantage is real but is
constant/poly-factor engineering with substantial prior art; we position it
accordingly.
\end{abstract}

\section{Motivation}
\texttt{clifft}'s state is split into (i) a \emph{symbolic Clifford frame}
evolving dormant axes for free, and (ii) a \emph{dense active block}, a $2^k$
statevector expanded only for non-Clifford content. A static profiler
(\texttt{research/stabrank\_profiling}) established two facts that scope this
work: $k$ is built from magic (plain Clifford superposition never inflates it),
and \texttt{clifft}'s measurement-reordering passes already shrink $k$
aggressively. The bet: when the active block is \emph{magic-sparse}, its
stabilizer rank is $\ll 2^k$ and a low-rank residual extends \texttt{clifft}'s
reach --- at the cost of exactness.

\section{Background and related work}
\paragraph{CH-form and low-rank decompositions.}
A stabilizer state is stored as $\ket{\phi}=\omega\,U_C U_H \ket{s}$
(Bravyi--Browne--Calpin--Campbell--Gosset--Howard~\cite{bravyi2019}): $O(n^2)$
bits per term, $O(n)$ Clifford gates, $O(n^2)$ Hadamard and single-amplitude
queries. A magic state is a sum $\ket\psi=\sum_a c_a\ket{\phi_a}$ of $\chi$
terms; Cliffords preserve $\chi$, each $T$ doubles it, measurement can collapse
it.

\paragraph{Related work (what is and is not new here).}
None of the individual ingredients is novel, and we position the composition
against its prior art explicitly. ``Cliffords paid once, exponential cost only
on the magic'' is the architecture of Bravyi--Gosset~\cite{bravyi2016} already;
Qassim, Wallman and Gosset~\cite{qassim2019} recompile circuits into
non-Clifford rotations times a single global Clifford precisely to speed up
CH-form simulators; Garc\'ia--Markov~\cite{garcia2015} shared a stabilizer
frame across superposition terms a decade ago; Pauli-based
computation~\cite{peres2023} absorbs all Cliffords into adaptive Pauli
measurements on $t$ magic qubits. The closest single work is Pashayan et
al.~\cite{pashayan2022}: gadgetize the $T$'s, then \emph{statically} compress
the global Clifford and the outcome projector into an effective magic register
before running a stabilizer-rank estimator. Stabilizer tensor networks with
magic injection~\cite{nakhl2025} pair a Clifford frame with an MPS residual;
\texttt{quizx}~\cite{kissinger2022} reaches the same ``decompose only the
magic'' endpoint via ZX rewriting. What this prototype adds is the
\emph{online} form of the composition: a persistent global frame maintained
gate-by-gate over a CH-form term sum, with \texttt{clifft}-style
measurement-driven active-subspace collapse, supporting mid-circuit and
adaptive measurement --- plus the engineering observation (verified in
qiskit-aer's source) that the flagship open-source CH-form simulator,
\texttt{extended\_stabilizer}, applies every Clifford per-term at $O(\chi)$
cost, with no frame. The advantage is a constant/poly factor, never an
exponent, and we claim nothing more for it.

\section{Method}

\subsection{Minimal-extent magic decomposition (the $0.228$ exponent)}
$T = \alpha I + \beta S$ with
$\alpha=\tfrac12+i\tfrac{\sqrt2-1}{2}$, $\beta=\bar\alpha$, both terms
Clifford, $|\alpha|+|\beta| = 2^{0.114}$, so the stabilizer extent per $T$ is
$2^{0.228}$ --- optimal within the extent framework, since extent is
multiplicative for tensor products of single-qubit states~\cite{bravyi2019}.
Branching in the computational basis instead costs extent $2^t$, which
sparsification cannot repair; this basis choice is the crux.

\subsection{Sparsification and single-shot magic sampling}
Importance-sampling $k$ terms from $p_a=|c_a|/\lVert c\rVert_1$ gives an
unbiased $\ket\omega$ with
$\mathbb{E}\lVert\ket\psi-\ket\omega\rVert^2=(\lVert c\rVert_1^2-\lVert\psi\rVert^2)/k$;
$k\sim 2^{0.228t}/\delta^2$ bounds the 2-norm error by $\delta$. For
\emph{product} magic (IQP's $\ket T^{\otimes n}$) the branch strings factorize
and we sample them directly --- unbiased, no $2^t$ built, and no factor-$t$
variance accumulation (streaming mid-circuit sparsification pays that factor;
it remains implemented but is not the benchmarked path).

\subsection{Norm estimation and normalization}\label{sec:norm}
$P(x)=|\bra x\psi\rangle|^2/\lVert\psi\rVert^2$ needs $\lVert\psi\rVert^2$
without materializing $2^n$; we implement the BGH estimator (Lemmas 2--4,
$O(n^3)$ exponential sum, validated exactly). Two honesty points the earlier
draft blurred. (i) The estimator's per-sample relative spread is $\approx\!1.2$,
so $L$ samples give $\approx\!1.2/\sqrt L$ relative error \emph{on every
reported probability}; at the $L=30$--$80$ used previously that is an
$11$--$22\%$ multiplicative error, the same order as the sparsification error
--- and the old ``norm-free TV'' metric cancelled it exactly. (ii) For the
benchmark family --- \emph{unitary} product-magic circuits ---
$\lVert\psi\rVert=1$ exactly and
$\mathbb{E}\lVert\omega\rVert^2 = 1+(\lVert c\rVert_1^2-1)/k$ is known
analytically, so normalization needs no estimation at all
(\texttt{samples=0} mode). We benchmark with analytic normalization and report
the estimated-norm mode separately; \emph{generic} circuits (projections,
non-product magic) must pay the estimator, whose cost to keep the norm error
subdominant scales as $\chi L \sim 2^{0.228t}/\delta^4$ --- a real limitation,
stated as such.

\subsection{Error guarantee, stated precisely}\label{sec:guarantee}
Sparsification bounds the \emph{2-norm} error
$\lVert\psi-\omega\rVert\le\delta$. For a single target that yields an
\emph{additive} amplitude error of typical size $\delta\,2^{-n/2}$ --- i.e.\ a
$\sim\!\delta$ \emph{relative} error on \emph{typical} (anticoncentrated) IQP
probabilities $P(x)\sim2^{-n}$, which is what the measured
$\mathrm{TV}\approx0.5\,\delta$ reflects. It is \textbf{not} a per-$x$
relative-error guarantee: individual small probabilities can be off by more.
Guaranteed relative error costs the exact-rank methods
($2^{0.396t}$~\cite{qassim2021}).

\subsection{Clifford-frame composition}
As in the earlier draft: $\ket{\mathrm{state}}=F(\sum_a\ket{\phi_a})$ with $F$
a global Clifford updated in $O(n)$ per gate; magic and measurement act on the
terms conjugated through $F$ at the optimal $\{I,S\}$ extent. Validated
against the plain engine (including forced-outcome measurement) to
$6\times10^{-15}$.

\section{The honest baseline}\label{sec:baseline}
The earlier draft timed \texttt{clifft.basis\_probabilities} on the
\emph{unitary} IQP program, forcing $\mathrm{peak\_rank}=n$. That is not how a
user computes $P(x)$: compiling the \emph{measured} program and calling
\texttt{record\_probabilities} (exact forced replay) exploits
\texttt{clifft}'s measurement-driven reduction. Measured facts
(\texttt{validate\_mitm.py}, review session):
\begin{itemize}
\item On the old benchmark's nearest-neighbour-CZ IQP the measured program
compiles to $\mathrm{peak\_rank}=1$ (lightcone sweep):
\texttt{record\_probabilities} returns the same $96$ exact probabilities in
$0.2$\,ms at $n{=}26$ --- vs the $23$\,s the old benchmark charged
\texttt{clifft} and the $1.3$\,s our backend took. \textbf{The old crossover
was an artifact of the baseline.}
\item On \emph{dense} random IQP (CZ on each pair w.p.\ $\tfrac12$, the
standard hard ensemble) the measured program compiles to
$\mathrm{peak\_rank}=n/2$: the honest exact baseline is $2^{n/2}$, not $2^n$.
\item Independently, a meet-in-the-middle (MitM) evaluator
(\texttt{chform\_cpp/mitm\_iqp.cpp}) computes exact $P(x)$ for any T$+$CZ IQP
in $O(n2^{n/2})$ time and $2^{n/2}$ memory --- ground truth to
$n\!\approx\!62$ on a $36$\,GB machine, validated against dense
($6\times10^{-16}$) and against \texttt{record\_probabilities}
($6\times10^{-14}$ at $n{=}24,30$).
\end{itemize}
So for this family, \emph{everything exact costs $2^{n/2}$}, and hardness
claims must be framed against that scale. (Multiplicative approximation
remains GapP-hard for T-type IQP~\cite{bremner2016}; there is no poly-time
escape, but $n{=}72$ is exactly checkable at $\sim\!2^{36}$ work --- by us.)

\section{Implementation and validation}
A Python prototype (\texttt{research/chform\_backend}) is the reference; a
bit-packed C\texttt{++}20 port (\texttt{research/chform\_cpp}) is the
performance implementation. This revision also fixed a latent bug: the C++
amplitude took a \texttt{uint64} target and shifted by qubit index ---
undefined behavior for $n>64$ (the very frontier sizes previously reported,
where it happened to work only for the all-zeros target). Amplitudes are now
word-based (\texttt{amplitude\_words}), and the multi-word ($n>64$) paths are
covered by new tests.

\section{Benchmarks}
All contestants run single-threaded on an Apple M-series workstation ($36$\,GB;
\texttt{clifft} uses its scalar/NEON path --- an x86 AVX-512 host would favor
\texttt{clifft}); the MitM ground truth uses all cores but competes with
no one. Scripts and the raw JSON are committed.

\subsection{Extent, sparsification, free Cliffords}
As before (unchanged, re-verified): measured $L_1$ growth per $T$ is exactly
$2^{0.114}$; sparsification error tracks the bound to $\sim\!1\%$; the
single-shot estimator is unbiased. On the measured magic-conveyor the frame
composition performs \textbf{zero} per-term Clifford operations vs
$473$--$15{,}411$ for a measurement-aware pure stabilizer-rank simulator
($w{=}4$--$8$) --- the constant-factor advantage of the composition,
\emph{cf.}~\cite{bravyi2016,qassim2019} for its static prior art.

\subsection{The honest crossover}\label{sec:overlap}

(cross-checked against \texttt{record\_probabilities} to $10^{-6}$ relative
everywhere both run); \texttt{clifft} baseline $=$ compile the measured

budget $k=2^{0.228n}/\delta^2$, analytic normalization (\S\ref{sec:norm}),

\subsection{The accuracy dial}\label{sec:precision}
At $n{=}44$, $256$ targets, $4$ realizations, analytic normalization
(Fig.~\ref{fig:honest}, right): $\mathrm{TV}=0.144(4),\,0.101(3),\,0.0500(6),\,
0.0251(3)$ at $\delta=0.30,0.20,0.10,0.05$ --- i.e.\
$\mathrm{TV}=(0.50\pm0.01)\,\delta$, with runtime $\propto k\propto1/\delta^2$
($2.0\to73.9$\,s). The earlier draft's ``$\mathrm{TV}\approx0.47\,\delta$'' was
approximately right, \emph{but only because its metric excluded the norm
error}: re-running the same budgets with the $L{=}30$ estimated norm (the old
setting) degrades same-budget TV by up to $\sim\!2\times$ on unlucky draws
($0.07$--$0.32$ observed vs $0.07$--$0.21$ analytic), exactly the
$1.2/\sqrt{30}\approx22\%$ multiplicative noise of \S\ref{sec:norm}. The clean
law holds for the full pipeline only where normalization is analytic (unitary
product magic) or the norm budget is scaled up ($\chi L\sim1/\delta^4$).

Dense IQP, $\delta{=}0.4$, single-shot build $+$ one amplitude
(\texttt{bench\_iqp.cpp}). The exact column is what \emph{any} known exact
method pays on this family ($2^{n/2}$: \texttt{clifft}-measured or MitM);
the old draft's ``$2^n$ / $64$\,ZB'' contrast overstated the gap by a factor
$2^{n/2}$.

Accuracy at the frontier: exact ground truth exists to $n\!\approx\!62$ (MitM),

checkable size, (ii) the analytic normalization being exact for this family,
and (iii) the $n{>}64$ code paths now being tested ($W{=}2$ rows of
Table~\ref{tab:valid}) --- an extrapolation, stated as such, not a

\subsection{Beyond product magic: gadgetized general circuits}\label{sec:gadget}
Every scaled result above uses the single-shot sampler, which needs all magic
in one product layer. The generalization to \emph{arbitrary} Clifford$+T$
circuits (\texttt{gadgetize.py}, C\texttt{++} arm
\texttt{bench\_gadget.cpp}): teleport each in-line $T$ onto its own ancilla
and force the gadget outcome to $0$ --- since the gadget's
classically-controlled correction makes all outcome branches equivalent, each
forced-$0$ gadget contributes exactly $T/\sqrt2$, so
$P(x) = 2^{t}\,|\bra{x,0^t} C_{\rm gadget} (\ket{0^n}\!\otimes\!\ket{T}^{\otimes t})|^2$
with $C_{\rm gadget}$ entirely Clifford. All magic is again one product
layer: the single-shot sampler applies with \textbf{no streaming $t$-factor},
and the normalization stays \emph{analytic} --- the norm-estimation
bottleneck of \S\ref{sec:norm} never enters. Validated: the $7T$ CCZ network
and exact gadgetized $=$ dense $=$ \texttt{clifft} to $10^{-14}$ on random
interleaved circuits; sparsified TV scales with $\delta$; the streaming
\texttt{sparsify} path is now also exercised (unbiased), closing that
coverage gap.

At scale, the hidden-shift family (bent-function construction, CCZ oracles,
$14$ $T$'s per CCZ) provides \emph{built-in exact ground truth}: the output
is the shift $s$ deterministically, so $P(s)=1$ at any size. Measured at
$\delta=0.3$: $n{=}16/24/32/40$ ($t=28$--$56$, up to $96$ total qubits)
give $\hat P(s) = 0.99/0.94/0.90/0.92$ in $0.1$--$8$\,s, with
$\hat P(x\!\neq\!s)=0$ --- interleaved magic handled at the product-magic
price.

Two honest observations. First, \texttt{clifft}'s measurement-driven
reduction compiles \emph{both} tested general families to tiny blocks
(hidden shift: $\mathrm{peak\_rank}\le10$; our random interleaved
Clifford$+T$: $\le6$) and answers exactly in microseconds --- these families
validate the backend's generality, they do not exhibit a regime where it
wins. Second, this sharpens into a \textbf{compile-time decision rule}: the
backend's exponent is $0.228\,t$, \texttt{clifft}'s is
$\mathrm{peak\_rank}$, and both are known \emph{before executing anything}
--- a hybrid dispatcher can route each program to the cheaper engine
($0.228\,t < \mathrm{peak\_rank}$: backend; otherwise \texttt{clifft}).
Dense IQP ($t=n$, $\mathrm{peak\_rank}=n/2$) sits on the backend's side, as
\S\ref{sec:overlap} measured; magic-dense or reduction-friendly circuits sit
on \texttt{clifft}'s. The rule must use the \emph{live} $T$-count after
\texttt{clifft}'s HIR optimization, not the raw one: measured on the random
interleaved family, $t_{\rm raw}=32/40/48$ compiles down to
$t_{\rm live}=18/28/28$ --- using $t_{\rm raw}$ biases the dispatch against
the backend.

\subsection{qiskit-aer \texttt{extended\_stabilizer}}\label{sec:aer}
Now reproduced by a committed script (\texttt{bench\_aer.py}; aer $0.17.2$,
settings inline --- the old draft's numbers were unauditable). Sampling
(nn-IQP, 2000 shots, mixing $50$): \texttt{clifft} samples exactly at
$1.8$--$4.4\times10^6$ shots/s ($\mathrm{peak\_rank}=1$) vs aer's approximate
$2721\to44$ shots/s over $n=10\to28$ --- ratios $1630\times$ to
$40{,}000\times$. Strong simulation (dense IQP $n{=}24$, 96 uniform targets,
true $P\sim5.6\times10^{-8}$): \texttt{clifft} answers exactly in $3.5$\,ms;
aer's only route is shot frequency, and $30{,}000$ shots ($455$\,s) hit
$0/96$ targets ($\sim\!2\times10^7$ shots needed per expected hit). The
three-way split stands: \texttt{clifft} owns exact work while $2^{n/2}$ fits;
this backend owns approximate $P(x)$ beyond; \texttt{extended\_stabilizer}
(sampling-only, maintenance-frozen upstream) is dominated on both tasks.

\subsection{External baselines: QuiZX (and Quokka\#)}\label{sec:external}
QuiZX~\cite{kissinger2022} (v0.3.0, PyPI wheel) computes each Born probability
\emph{exactly}, one ZX-simplify$+$decompose run per target, validated here
against MitM to $10^{-6}$ relative on every instance. On the SAME dense-IQP
instances and targets as \S\ref{sec:overlap} (\texttt{bench\_external.py}),
its per-amplitude cost grows as the exact-rank rate $2^{0.396n}$ (measured
term counts $301\to1.9\times10^6$ over $n{=}24\to56$, $\times9.0$ per 8
qubits: ZX simplification does \emph{not} compress dense T$+$CZ IQP), giving
for 96 targets: $0.5$\,s ($n{=}24$), $251$\,s ($n{=}48$), $2188$\,s
($n{=}56$) --- vs this backend's $0.3/17/89$\,s at $\mathrm{TV}\approx0.08$.
Two honest qualifiers. (1) QuiZX answers a \emph{harder} question (exact vs
additive-approximate); the comparison shows complementary regimes, not
dominance. (2) Our own MitM evaluator is the strongest \emph{exact} method on
this family --- $0.4/4.7/84.5$\,s for the same queries, i.e.\ it \emph{ties
the approximate backend through $n\!\approx\!56$} --- so on pure T$+$CZ IQP
the approximate backend's real niche over \emph{all} known exact methods only
opens past the $2^{n/2}$ memory wall ($n\gtrsim60$), or on circuit families
without MitM structure. Quokka\#~\cite{mei2024} (with its GPMC
model counter, built locally) was run on the same instances: exact
per-amplitude, $3.1$\,s at $n{=}24$ (correct to $5\times10^{-15}$) but
\emph{timeout} ($>300$\,s/amplitude) already at $n{=}32$ --- the dense CZ
graph defeats the CNF encoding far below the tool's published sparse-circuit
range. On this family the external exact ranking is QuiZX $\gg$ Quokka\#,
with our MitM evaluator fastest of all three.

\subsection{The adaptive workload: where the composition pays off ---
and where it does not}\label{sec:adaptive}
The composition's defensible novelty is \emph{online} operation: mid-circuit
measurement with classical feedforward. We benchmark an adaptive family
(\texttt{bench\_adaptive.py}): a width-$w$ register, $R{=}4$ rounds of
$H$-layer, feedforward-$X$ conditioned on the previous round's outcomes, a
$T^{\pm}$ layer, $D$ global Clifford scrambling layers applied \emph{while}
$\chi=2^w$, a CZ chain, $H$-layer, then measurement of all $w$ qubits.
Trajectories are sampled once (dense reference), then \emph{replayed} by both
engines --- identical circuits, identical outcomes, identical CH-form term
stores and measurement code; the only difference is who pays for Cliffords
(plain: per-term, the verified architecture of Aer's
\texttt{extended\_stabilizer}; frame: $O(n)$ absorption). All engine variants
agree to $3\times10^{-16}$.

Three findings, two of them not in the composition's favor:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{The incumbent cannot enter.} qiskit-aer
\texttt{extended\_stabilizer} \emph{rejects} the workload outright at every
size (dynamic-circuit \texttt{mark}/\texttt{jump} instructions unsupported).
Online adaptive simulation at the CH-form representation is territory the
flagship open-source implementation does not serve at all.
\item \textbf{Free Cliffords are real but not free lunch.} At $w{=}12$,
$D{=}4$: the plain engine spends $68$\,s applying Cliffords per-term where the
frame spends $3$\,ms --- but the frame engine \emph{loses overall} ($217$\,s
vs $77$\,s), because frame-conjugated magic and measurement act through
$P'=F^{-1}Z_qF$ of weight $\sim w$, costing $O(w)$ per-term gate applications
per $T$ and per measurement. The frame does not eliminate per-term work; it
\emph{moves} it from Cliffords onto magic and measurement.
\item \textbf{The measured phase boundary.} Sweeping $D$ at $w{=}8$: frame
time is \emph{flat} ($6.9$--$7.9$\,s from $D{=}4$ to $96$) while plain grows
linearly ($3.1\to65.9$\,s); the crossover sits at $D^*\!\approx\!10\approx1.2w$,
and at $D{=}96$ the frame is $8.4\times$ faster and the gap grows linearly in
$D$. \textbf{The online composition pays off precisely when the adaptive
circuit is Clifford-dominated} ($\gtrsim w$ Clifford layers per magic/measure
round --- syndrome-extraction-like traffic), and costs $\sim2\times$ overhead
when it is not.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Natural workloads land on the winning side.}
The synthetic sweep leaves one question: do \emph{recognizable} protocols sit
above or below $D^*$? Two natural adaptive families
(\texttt{bench\_natural.py}; trajectories sampled once on a dense reference,
replayed identically by both engines; all variants agree to $10^{-16}$):
\emph{(i) cultivation-style patches} --- a data register accumulates injected
$T$'s (never measured away) while every round runs syndrome extraction
(ancilla CX fans, measurements, classically-controlled corrections, ancilla
reuse) plus $L$ layers of code-preserving logical Clifford traffic
(deformation/surgery); \emph{(ii) teleported-$T$ injection} --- the textbook
adaptive magic gadget (ancilla $\ket T$, CX, measure, classically-controlled
$S$ correction), the minimal-Clifford contrast point. Measured (8 data
qubits, 7 checks, up to 10 injected $T$'s, $\chi$ up to $\sim$$10^3$):

\begin{table}[h]\centering
\caption{Natural adaptive workloads: plain (per-term Cliffords) vs frame,
identical trajectories.}\label{tab:natural}
\begin{tabular}{lrr}
\toprule
workload & Cliffords/round & frame speedup \\
\midrule
bare syndrome extraction ($L{=}0$) & $\sim$14 & $0.8$--$1.0\times$ (at the boundary) \\
$+$ 1 logical-traffic layer & $\sim$32 & $3.7$--$6.7\times$ \\
$+$ 4 layers & $\sim$68 & $7$--$16\times$ \\
teleported-$T$ gadget & $\sim$4/gadget & $1.7$--$2.8\times$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Bare syndrome extraction sits \emph{exactly at} the measured boundary, and
any logical Clifford traffic at all pushes the composition into clear wins ---
the plain engine's per-term Clifford work is the entire gap (e.g.\ $11.8$\,s
of a $12.0$\,s round set vs the frame's $7$\,ms). Even the minimal teleported
gadget benefits, because the frame absorbs its H/CX while $\chi$ is large.
One physical subtlety the experiment surfaced: the logical traffic must be
\emph{code-preserving} (diagonal $+$ CNOT-type; no bare $H$ on data), else
the syndrome round measures the accumulated magic away --- true of the toy
and of the real protocols it models.

\begin{figure}[h]\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{chform_cpp/external_adaptive.png}
\caption{\emph{Left:} external head-to-head on shared dense-IQP instances:
QuiZX (exact, per-target) vs the MitM evaluator (exact) vs this backend
(approximate, $\mathrm{TV}\approx0.08$), seconds for 96 probabilities.
\emph{Right:} the adaptive-workload phase boundary at $w{=}8$: plain
(per-term Cliffords) grows linearly in Clifford depth $D$; the frame
composition is flat; crossover at $D^*\!\approx\!1.2w$.}
\label{fig:extadapt}
\end{figure}

\section{The conceptual frame: one compiler, two executors}\label{sec:arch}
The results above assemble into a single architecture, and it is worth
stating plainly, because it also settles what this backend \emph{is} relative
to \texttt{clifft}.

\paragraph{What comes from where.} The backend borrows \texttt{clifft}'s two
architectural ideas --- the global symbolic Clifford frame (absorb Cliffords
in $O(n)$, keep the non-Clifford core small) and measurement-driven collapse
of that core --- and re-instantiates them over a different core: BGH's
low-rank CH-form sum instead of a dense $2^k$ array. The simulation
mathematics (CH-form, minimal-extent decomposition, sparsification, norm
estimation, gadgetization) is BGH/Bravyi--Gosset throughout; none of
\texttt{clifft}'s runtime is used. \texttt{clifft} appears in three
supporting roles: validation oracle (every component is checked against it
to machine precision), the honest benchmark opponent, and --- the role that
matters going forward --- the \emph{compiler front-end}.

\paragraph{Compile once, dispatch per program.} Both executors' cost
exponents are known from the compiled artifact before anything runs:
\texttt{clifft}'s dense engine pays $2^{\mathrm{peak\_rank}}$ (the
$k$-schedule is compile-time static), and the CH-form backend pays
$\sim 2^{0.228\,t}/\delta^2$ (the live $T$-count survives the same
compilation). Dispatch is a one-line comparison:

\begin{center}
\begin{tikzpicture}[
  box/.style={draw, rounded corners=1pt, inner sep=6pt, font=\small},
  sub/.style={font=\scriptsize, color=black!60},
  lbl/.style={font=\scriptsize\itshape}]
  \node[box] (circ) at (0,0) {circuit};
  \node[box] (comp) at (3.0,0) {\texttt{clifft} compiler};
  \node[box] (meta) at (6.6,0) {compiled program};
  \node[sub] at (6.6,-0.55) {$\mathrm{peak\_rank}$, $t_{\rm live}$};
  \node[box] (dense) at (12.0,1.35) {dense engine};
  \node[sub] at (12.0,0.80) {exact, $2^{\mathrm{peak\_rank}}$};
  \node[box] (chf) at (12.0,-1.35) {CH-form backend};
  \node[sub] at (12.0,-1.90) {$\delta$-approx., $2^{0.228 t}/\delta^2$};
  \draw[->] (circ) -- (comp);
  \draw[->] (comp) -- (meta);
  \draw[->] (meta.east) to[out=25,in=180] (dense.west);
  \draw[->] (meta.east) to[out=-25,in=180] (chf.west);
  \node[lbl] at (9.35,0.95) {$0.228\,t \ge \mathrm{peak\_rank}$};
  \node[lbl] at (9.35,-0.95) {$0.228\,t < \mathrm{peak\_rank}$ (opt-in $\delta$)};
\end{tikzpicture}
\end{center}

This is no longer only a proposal: the backend now \textbf{consumes
\texttt{clifft}'s optimized HIR directly} (\texttt{hir\_bridge.py}, using the
exposed \texttt{parse}$\to$\texttt{trace}$\to$\texttt{HirPassManager}
pipeline). The optimized HIR turns out to be the ideal input, for a reason
worth stating: \emph{it contains no Clifford gates at all} --- the compiler
absorbs every Clifford into the Pauli strings of the surviving ops, i.e.\ it
performs the frame absorption \emph{statically and exactly}. The remaining
ops are precisely the backend's two explicit-Pauli primitives ($T$-rotations
about arbitrary Paulis; projective Pauli measurements), so the bridge is
thin. Validated against \texttt{clifft} to $2\times10^{-13}$ over 400 fuzzed
circuits plus the benchmark families; in every HIR-driven run the backend
performs \emph{zero} Clifford gate applications, $\chi$ tracks
$2^{t_{\rm live}}$ (often less: the hoisted measurements collapse terms
mid-run --- $\chi_{\rm peak}=8$ where $2^{t_{\rm live}}=64$ on one family),
and $t_{\rm live}$ is roughly half of $t_{\rm raw}$ on random circuits.
Consequently, for compile-known circuits the compiler \emph{supersedes} the
online frame of \S\ref{sec:adaptive}; the online frame remains the mechanism
for dynamic/adaptive circuits the compiler cannot see through. The
C\texttt{++} scale arm still consumes raw circuits (consuming HIR there
needs a simultaneous reduction of the terminal Pauli measurements --- a
symplectic elimination --- noted as future work).

Three design consequences. \emph{(i) Both executors want the same compiled
stream.} Every compiler improvement ($T$-count reduction, fusion, measurement
reordering) lowers both engines' costs --- now demonstrated, not assumed:
the Python reference consumes the optimized stream; only the C\texttt{++}
arm's numbers remain conservative. \emph{(ii) The
dispatcher must respect the exactness contract.} The backend is a different
guarantee ($\delta$-approximate, additive/typical --- \S\ref{sec:guarantee}),
so it is an opt-in path (an explicit $\delta$), never a silent substitute:
when the user demands exactness past the memory wall, the honest answer is
``infeasible''. \emph{(iii) The finer-grained, per-episode rule is
implemented} (\texttt{dispatch.py}). Compiled programs have episode
structure ($k$ rising and collapsing to $0$); the static profiler supplies
$m_{\rm blk}$ (peak $T$-count inside any single episode) and the episode
count $R$, and the dispatcher weighs a third strategy: re-sparsify at every
episode boundary, cost $\sim R^2\,2^{0.228\,m_{\rm blk}}/\delta^2$ (errors
compound over $R$ boundaries, so $\delta_{\rm episode}=\delta/\sqrt R$).
Since $m_{\rm blk}\le t_{\rm live}$, this only moves circuits toward the
backend --- decisively for computations that \emph{recycle} bounded live
magic: on a feedforward conveyor with $12$ rounds of $128$ $T$'s, the dense
engine is infeasible ($k{=}49$), the global backend absurd
($0.228\cdot1536\approx350$), and the episodic strategy ($\log_2$ cost
$\approx42$) is the only one that runs --- the dispatcher selects it
automatically. The premise is validated in exact mode
($\chi_{\rm peak}\approx2^{m_{\rm blk}}\ll2^{t_{\rm live}}$ on a conveyor
via the HIR bridge, which now also replays the feedforward's conditional
Paulis; $P$ matches \texttt{clifft} to $4\times10^{-17}$). The approximate episodic execution is now \emph{implemented and
measured} (\texttt{bench\_episodic.py}), and the measurements refine the
strategy into two: \textbf{episodic-exact} --- budget at the per-episode
rank $2^{m_{\rm blk}}$, giving \emph{zero} error at cost exponent
$m_{\rm blk}$ instead of $t_{\rm live}$ (measured:
$\chi_{\rm peak}=2^{m_{\rm blk}}$, $P$ exactly matching \texttt{clifft})
--- and \textbf{episodic-approximate} below that budget. The sound
approximate schedule took two measured corrections: never resample after a
projection (forced measurements inflate $\lVert c\rVert_1/\lVert\psi\rVert$
and make the BGH resample ill-conditioned --- this alone was a $24\times$
error), and debias with the cross product of two independent runs
($\mathbb{E}\langle\Pi\omega|\Pi\omega'\rangle=\lVert\Pi\psi\rVert^2$;
measured bias $-0.004$ vs the naive estimator's $+1.7$ at aggressive
budgets). So configured, a $72$-qubit conveyor ($t_{\rm live}=72$,
exact-mode $\chi=2^{72}$) runs end-to-end with no $2^n$ object at
$\chi\le400$ and relative error $0.4$ at $10\times$ per-episode
compression. The honest limit, also measured: for \emph{full-record}
probabilities (exponentially small targets) the error turns on sharply below
the exact budget and compounds steeply with $R$ --- the $R^2$ cost model is
optimistic there; use episodic-exact or mild compression for record targets.
The dispatcher weighs all four strategies.

In one sentence: \texttt{clifft}'s architecture is the blueprint, BGH's
mathematics is the material, and \texttt{clifft} itself is the compiler
front-end that decides --- per program, before execution --- whether the
dense exact engine or the low-rank approximate backend runs.

\section{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Approximate}, with the guarantee of \S\ref{sec:guarantee}
(additive/typical, not per-$x$ relative), and \texttt{clifft}'s exactness
forfeited.
\item \textbf{The exact competition is $2^{n/2}$, not $2^n$}, on this family;
the backend's genuinely-unique regime starts near $n\!\approx\!62$, and its
speed advantage at moderate accuracy starts near $n\!\approx\!34$--$48$.
\item \textbf{Norm estimation} is the pipeline's accuracy-cost bottleneck for
generic circuits ($\chi L\sim1/\delta^4$); the clean results here lean on
analytic normalization, valid for unitary product magic only.
\item \textbf{The composition's value is measured and two-sided, and natural
protocols land on the winning side} (\S\ref{sec:adaptive},
Table~\ref{tab:natural}): the frame wins iff the circuit is
Clifford-dominated while $\chi$ is large ($D^*\!\approx\!1.2w$ on the
synthetic sweep); bare syndrome extraction sits at the boundary, and
cultivation-style workloads with any logical Clifford traffic win
$4$--$16\times$ (teleported-$T$ gadgets $\sim\!2\times$). The conjugation of
magic and measurement through the frame remains the price of free Cliffords.
Prior art for the static forms
remains~\cite{bravyi2016,qassim2019,garcia2015,pashayan2022}.
\item \textbf{Prototype gaps:} the Python engine's sampling measurement path
and canonical dedup materialize $2^n$ (validation-scale; the forced-replay
path, \texttt{measure\_z\_forced\_fast} $+$ \texttt{collapse\_to\_rank1}, is
non-materialising); the C\texttt{++} engine has no measurement path
(build-and-query only; the gadgetized route, \S\ref{sec:gadget}, removes the
need for mid-circuit measurement in strong simulation). The adaptive
wall-clock numbers are Python-vs-Python (fair internally, absolute constants
not comparable to C\texttt{++} tools).
\item \texttt{quEStab} (ACM ICS 2026, multi-GPU extended stabilizer) still
needs a manual literature check (paywalled, no preprint).
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}
The validated machinery stands, and so does a real --- but honestly smaller
--- niche. Against \texttt{clifft}'s true exact fast path on dense IQP, the
CH-form backend wins from $n\!\approx\!34$ (coarse) / $n\!\approx\!48$
($\mathrm{TV}\!\approx\!0.08$), and past $n\!\approx\!62$ it is the only
method of the three (dense block, forced replay, MitM) that runs at all:
$n{=}72$ in $267$\,s and $1.9$\,GB where anything exact needs
$\sim\!1$\,TB. The accuracy dial is clean and predictable
($\mathrm{TV}=0.50\,\delta$) once normalization is handled honestly. What
this note deliberately no longer claims: a crossover at $n\!\approx\!22$
(baseline artifact), $2^n$-scale frontier contrasts ($2^{n/2}$ is the honest
exact scale), sub-$10\%$ accuracy at budgets whose norm error exceeded that
(metric artifact), and novelty for free Cliffords as an idea (prior art).

The follow-up experiments are now done, each with a two-sided answer.
\emph{External baselines} (\S\ref{sec:external}): the backend beats QuiZX's
exact per-target cost by growing margins ($2188$\,s vs $89$\,s at $n{=}56$ for
96 targets, exact vs $\mathrm{TV}\approx0.08$), but our own exact MitM
evaluator ties the backend through $n\!\approx\!56$ --- on pure T$+$CZ IQP the
approximate niche opens only past the $2^{n/2}$ wall or off the IQP structure.
\emph{The adaptive workload} (\S\ref{sec:adaptive}): the incumbent CH-form
implementation cannot run adaptive circuits at all; the online frame
composition is flat in Clifford depth where per-term simulation grows
linearly, winning beyond a measured phase boundary $D^*\!\approx\!1.2w$ ---
and losing $\sim2\times$ below it, because frame conjugation shifts per-term
cost onto magic and measurement. Crucially, \emph{natural} protocols land on
the winning side (Table~\ref{tab:natural}): cultivation-style patches with
logical Clifford traffic win $4$--$16\times$, teleported-$T$ gadgets
$\sim\!2\times$, and only bare syndrome extraction sits at the boundary. The
composition is a real, now-quantified advantage precisely for the
fault-tolerance-shaped circuits it was designed for. Architecturally, the
pieces assemble into one compiler with two executors chosen at compile time
(\S\ref{sec:arch}).
